name: D-aspartic acid (DAA)

card.summary: An amino acid sold as a testosterone booster; early work suggested a hormonal role, but trials in trained men found no increase and, at higher intake, a decrease.
card.note: Three randomized trials in resistance-trained men reported no testosterone increase; one reported lower testosterone at the higher intake tested.

quick.overview:
D-aspartic acid is the mirror-image (D-form) of the common amino acid aspartic acid, found naturally in the pituitary gland and testes. It is sold as a sports supplement marketed for raising testosterone.
A 2009 study reported that sodium D-aspartate increased luteinizing hormone and testosterone in humans and rats. Later randomized trials in resistance-trained men found no testosterone rise, and one found lower testosterone at 6 grams per day.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work in rats proposes that D-aspartate acts in the pituitary to increase LH release and in testicular Leydig cells to raise testosterone synthesis, via cGMP and cAMP signaling. Human trials in trained men did not show this effect.
quick.risks: The trials report no major safety signals, but one reported lower total and free testosterone with 6 g/day, and another reported a 16 percent drop in estradiol. It is sold as a dietary supplement; long-term safety data are limited.

lead: D-aspartic acid (DAA) is the D-enantiomer of aspartic acid, one of two D-amino acids commonly found in mammals; it is concentrated in tissues including the pituitary gland and testes and is not built into proteins in the usual way [1][2]. It is sold as a dietary supplement, often in testosterone-support and pre-workout blends, and lifters take it with the aim of raising testosterone to support muscle growth, strength and recovery, and through that a fuller, leaner physique.

The appeal rests on a 2009 report from an Italian group that sodium D-aspartate raised luteinizing hormone (LH) and testosterone in humans and rats [2][12]. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials in resistance-trained men published between 2013 and 2017 reported no rise in testosterone, and one reported lower testosterone at the higher intake tested [3][4][5]. A 2017 systematic review of 23 animal and 4 human studies found raised testosterone in male animals but inconsistent human findings, and a 2024 systematic review of 27 proposed testosterone boosters, which included two DAA studies, concluded that most failed to raise total testosterone versus placebo [13][6]. A small 2025 trial in men with idiopathic infertility, using a combination of DAA, ubiquinol and zinc, reported higher testosterone and sperm motility after three months [7].

On the T Nation forum, DAA appears in supplement stacks, in discussions of post-cycle recovery and in threads from men with low testosterone results, where some members report using it and others question the research behind it [8][9][10][15][16].
infobox: Powder or capsule, alone or in blends

paras: Aspartic acid occurs in two mirror-image forms. Wikipedia reports that the L-form, discovered in 1827 by Auguste-Arthur Plisson and Etienne-Ossian Henry from asparagine, is the one used to make proteins, while the D-form is one of only two D-amino acids commonly found in mammals and acts as a neurotransmitter or neuromodulator with more limited biological roles [1].

Supplement products contain D-aspartic acid as a powder or in capsules, either alone or inside testosterone-support and pre-workout blends sold to lifters. Healthline describes it as commonly included in testosterone-boosting supplements [14].

The 2009 paper in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology, by Enza Topo, Gemma D'Aniello and colleagues in Naples, noted that D-aspartate had been found in neuroendocrine tissues of invertebrates and vertebrates and had been linked to GnRH, LH and growth hormone release in rats, but had not been tested for effects on LH and testosterone in humans [12].

In the human part of that study, 23 men aged 27 to 37 took a sodium D-aspartate solution each morning for 12 days while 20 men took a placebo. At day 12 LH had risen from 4.2 to 5.6 mIU/ml and testosterone from 4.5 to 6.4 ng/ml, about a 42 percent rise; testosterone was still elevated three days after stopping, and the placebo group showed no change [12]. In rats given D-aspartate in drinking water, LH and testosterone rose and D-aspartate accumulated most in the pituitary and testes [12]. The authors noted the small sample and short duration, and wrote that the supplement was marketed by a company although they declared no competing interests [12].
That 42 percent figure became the headline number in supplement marketing and in popular articles, which Healthline summarises alongside the later trials in trained men [14].

The 2009 study reported that the pituitary and testes synthesize D-aspartate from L-aspartate via a racemase enzyme and take it up efficiently. In rat pituitary tissue it increased LH release and synthesis via cGMP signaling, and in rat Leydig cells it increased testosterone synthesis and release via cAMP; L-aspartate did not raise LH or testosterone in rats [12]. Aspartate-related compounds such as NMDA act on glutamate receptors in the nervous system, and D-aspartate is also described as a neuromodulator [1].
The 2009 report combined a human component, in which sodium D-aspartate was associated with higher LH and testosterone, with rat experiments [2][12].

In a 2013 trial, resistance-trained men took 3 g of DAA or placebo for 28 days alongside heavy training; total and free testosterone, LH, GnRH and estradiol were unchanged, and strength and body composition changes did not differ between groups [3]. A 2015 trial randomized 24 trained men to placebo, 3 g or 6 g daily for 14 days: 3 g did not differ from placebo, while total testosterone was lower in the 6 g group and free testosterone was lower than placebo [4]. A 2017 randomized trial in 22 trained men over 12 weeks of supervised training at 6 g daily found no change in total or free testosterone, a 16 percent fall in estradiol, and similar training outcomes in both groups; its authors wrote that DAA was ineffective at changing testosterone [5].

A 2017 systematic review searching databases through October 2015 included 23 animal studies and 4 human studies; it reported that exogenous D-aspartic acid raised testosterone in male animals, with effects varying by species and organ, that human findings were inconsistent and that the human evidence was sparse, and its authors called for larger, longer, well-designed human trials [13]. Healthline's summary of the literature reports that the studies showing increases involved healthy or middle-aged men with lower starting testosterone, while active, weight-training men showed no increase and no extra muscle or strength [14].

The 2024 systematic review of testosterone boosters in athletes, healthy men, men with late-onset hypogonadism and infertile men covered 52 studies and reported that most of the 27 supplements examined, DAA among them, did not raise total testosterone versus placebo [6]. In a 2025 randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 75 men with idiopathic infertility, a daily combination of 2660 mg DAA, ubiquinol and zinc was associated with higher progressive sperm motility and total testosterone at three months; the product was a combination, so the contribution of DAA alone was not separated [7]. Healthline also describes a study of 60 men with fertility problems in which three months of DAA was followed by higher sperm count and motility [14].

The trials above did not report serious adverse events, but did report changes in hormone levels: lower total and free testosterone with 6 g/day in one trial, and reduced estradiol in another [4][5]. Healthline notes that most studies did not report side effects, that one small study recorded irritability, headaches and nervousness in a few men on DAA and in one on placebo, and that a 90-day study with blood testing reported no safety concerns [14]. No long-term safety studies are available.

subs.h: Use in lifting and bodybuilding forums
paras: DAA is sold in the US as a dietary supplement, typically as a powder or in capsule blends marketed to lifters. It appears in T Nation supplement logs, in threads asking whether it helps men with low testosterone readings, and in post-cycle recovery discussions [8][9][10][15][16]. In a 2008 prohormone thread a member listed DAA in a planned post-cycle routine alongside other supplements [8]. A member of a 2010 thread summarized early animal work on D-form amino acids and wondered whether it applied to lifters [9]; in a 2011 contest-prep thread a lifter listed DAA among his supplements [16]; in a 2019 thread a member advised another with low testosterone to take DAA and ashwagandha, describing both as clinically proven [10]. Another 2019 poster who had taken a box of DAA for about two weeks before bloodwork wrote that free testosterone was higher than at a previous test, while also taking magnesium, zinc and other supplements [15].
DAA is sold alone and in blends with ingredients such as zinc, magnesium, vitamin D and herbal extracts. The 2025 fertility trial used a product combining DAA, ubiquinol and zinc [7].

lore.intro: On T Nation, DAA is discussed as one of several over-the-counter testosterone supports, alongside zinc, magnesium and herbal extracts, in supplement logs, post-cycle recovery threads and low-testosterone threads [8][9][10][15][16].

claims.believers: Members cite the 2009 human and rat report and describe taking it when testosterone looked low, with one 2019 poster calling it clinically proven to boost testosterone [10][2].
claims.experts: Randomized trials in resistance-trained men reported no increase, and one reported lower testosterone at 6 g per day; a 2024 systematic review reached a similar overall finding for most boosters [3][4][5][6].

claims.claim: DAA helps recovery after a cycle of anabolic compounds
claims.believers: Threads from 2008 and 2012 discuss adding DAA to post-cycle routines to help restore natural testosterone [8][11].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested DAA in men recovering from anabolic steroid or prohormone use.

claims.claim: DAA supports fertility and sperm quality
claims.believers: Some users and supplement makers point to its presence in testes and to small studies in infertile men.
claims.experts: A 2025 randomized trial of a DAA, ubiquinol and zinc combination in infertile men reported higher motility and testosterone; it was a single combination study [7].

claims.believers: The figure comes from the 2009 human arm, in which testosterone rose from 4.5 to 6.4 ng/ml after 12 days; supplement marketing and some posters cite it [12][14].
claims.experts: The study enrolled 23 men and its authors noted the small sample and short duration; later trials in trained men did not reproduce a rise [12][3][4][5].

claims.claim: DAA works best in men with low or ordinary baseline testosterone, not in trained lifters
claims.believers: Forum members and some summaries say the effect shows up in men who are not training hard or who have lower starting levels [14][10].
claims.experts: Healthline's summary reports increases in some inactive or middle-aged men and none in active weight-training men; the 2017 review called human data inconsistent and sparse [14][13].

claims.believers: Lifters take it as part of stacks aimed at muscle gain and recovery [16][8].
claims.experts: In the 28-day and 12-week trials, strength and body composition changes were the same with DAA and with placebo [3][5].

claims.claim: Stacking DAA with ashwagandha raises low testosterone
claims.believers: A 2019 T Nation reply recommends both and advises re-testing after three months [10].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested this pairing; DAA trials in trained men did not show a rise on their own [3][4][5].
